claim: C. elegans contains 19 functional AGO proteins
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans contains an expanded family of 19 functional AGO proteins, many of which have not been fully characterized.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the systematic analysis throughout the manuscript showing 19 AGOs were characterized

claim: AGOs are the core components of ribonucleoprotein complexes called RISCs
source: AGOs are the core components of ribonucleoprotein complexes called RISCs (RNA induced silencing complexes) and are guided in a sequence-specific manner by sRNAs (18–30 nucleotides long) to complementary target transcripts (Dueck and Meister, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dueck and Meister, 2014

claim: AGOs have a bilobed structure consisting of four major domains: PAZ, MID, PIWI, and a low-complexity N-terminal domain
source: AGOs have a bilobed structure consisting of four major domains: PAZ, MID, PIWI, and a low-complexity N-terminal domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AGO protein structure

claim: The PAZ and MID domains possess pockets to coordinate 3′ and 5′ end sRNA binding, respectively
source: The PAZ and MID domains possess pockets to coordinate 3′ and 5′ end sRNA binding, respectively (Sheu-Gruttadauria and MacRae, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sheu-Gruttadauria and MacRae, 2017

claim: The PIWI domain resembles RNaseH and has the capacity to direct endonucleolytic cleavage of the target RNA if the active site harbors a tetrad of catalytic amino acids (DEDD/H)
source: The PIWI domain resembles RNaseH and has the capacity to direct endonucleolytic cleavage of the target RNA if the active site harbors a tetrad of catalytic amino acids (DEDD/H, Nakanishi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nakanishi et al., 2012

claim: Relatively few AGOs possess the catalytic tetrad required for endonucleolytic cleavage
source: Relatively few AGOs possess this catalytic tetrad, and many AGOs recruit additional proteins to elicit other gene regulatory outcomes, such as mRNA de-capping, de-adenylation, or chromatin modulation.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about AGO proteins

claim: C. elegans has at least four types of endogenous sRNAs: miRNAs, piRNAs, 22G-RNAs, and 26G-RNAs
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, at least four types of endogenous sRNAs—miRNAs, piRNAs, 22G-RNAs, and 26G-RNAs—and as many as 27 AGO-like genes have the potential to contribute to complex networks of gene regulation in different tissues throughout development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. elegans sRNA types

claim: miRNAs and piRNAs are genomically encoded and transcribed by RNA polymerase II
source: miRNAs and piRNAs are genomically encoded and transcribed by RNA polymerase II, while the 22G-RNAs and 26G-RNAs are generated by the activity of different RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRPs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about sRNA biogenesis

claim: 22G-RNAs and 26G-RNAs are generated by the activity of different RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRPs)
source: miRNAs and piRNAs are genomically encoded and transcribed by RNA polymerase II, while the 22G-RNAs and 26G-RNAs are generated by the activity of different RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRPs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about sRNA biogenesis

claim: miRNAs associate and function with the conserved AGOs ALG-1, ALG-2, and ALG-5
source: miRNAs are known to associate and function with the conserved AGOs ALG-1, ALG-2, and ALG-5 (Hutvagner et al., 2004; Brown et al., 2017; Corrêa et al., 2010; Vasquez-Rifo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations

claim: piRNAs bind to the PIWI AGO PRG-1
source: The Piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs, also called 21U-RNAs in C. elegans) bind to the PIWI AGO PRG-1 and are thought to maintain germline genome integrity by silencing foreign or deleterious nucleic acids such as transgenes (Lee et al., 2012; Shirayama et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2012 and Shirayama et al., 2012

claim: piRNA pathways are broadly and consistently required in animal germlines to ensure fertility
source: Although piRNA pathways in other animals play a more prominent role in regulating transposable elements than in C. elegans, the functions of the piRNA pathway are broadly and consistently required in animal germlines to ensure fertility (Ozata et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ozata et al., 2019

claim: 26G-RNAs are synthesized by the RdRP RRF-3
source: The 26G-RNAs are synthesized by the RdRP RRF-3, which generates dsRNA that is processed into 26G-RNAs by the endonuclease DICER and the phosphatase PIR-1 (Chaves et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chaves et al., 2021

claim: 26G-RNAs are classified into two groups: class I of spermatogenic origin (associated with ALG-3 and ALG-4) and class II of oogenic and embryonic origin (associated with ERGO-1)
source: 26G-RNAs are classified into two groups: those of spermatogenic origin (class I, associated with ALG-3 and ALG-4, Han et al., 2009; Conine et al., 2010) and those of oogenic and embryonic origin (class II, associated with ERGO-1, Vasale et al., 2010; Han et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations

claim: 22G-RNAs are generated by the RdRPs RRF-1 and EGO-1, independent of DICER
source: The 22G-RNAs are generated by the RdRPs RRF-1 and EGO-1, independent of DICER.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about 22G-RNA biogenesis

claim: CSR-1-bound 22G-RNAs target germline expressed protein-coding transcripts to protect them from silencing
source: Currently, 22G-RNAs are divided into two main groups, those that are bound by CSR-1 and target germline expressed protein-coding transcripts to protect them from silencing, along with fine-tuning gene expression in the embryo (Claycomb et al., 2009; Cecere et al., 2014; Seth et al., 2013; Wedeles et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2021; Gerson-Gurwitz et al., 2016; Nguyen and Phillips, 2021; Charlesworth et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations

claim: WAGO class AGOs (such as WAGO-1 and HRDE-1) silence protein-coding genes, pseudogenes, transposable elements, and cryptic loci
source: versus those that are bound by other WAGO class AGOs (such as WAGO-1 and HRDE-1) that silence protein-coding genes, pseudogenes, transposable elements, and cryptic loci (Gu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gu et al., 2009

claim: Previous studies identified 27 ago genes in C. elegans
source: Previous studies identified 27 ago genes in C. elegans (Yigit et al., 2006); however, some have been reclassified as pseudogenes (e.g., prg-2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yigit et al., 2006

claim: 21 genes in C. elegans contain PAZ and PIWI domains, have a predicted protein size of ~100 kDa, and bear homology to known AGOs
source: To define an updated set of ago genes to study, we searched the genome (WormBase version WS262) for genes that contain PAZ and PIWI domains, have a predicted protein size of ~100 kDa, and bear homology to known AGOs. Twenty-one genes met these criteria, and we ultimately characterized 19 of these AGOs
evidence: This is based on the authors' computational search of the genome

claim: Seven C. elegans AGOs belong to the AGO clade: ALG-1, ALG-2, ALG-3, ALG-4, ALG-5, ERGO-1, and RDE-1
source: Construction of a phylogenetic tree for these 19 AGOs in relation to Arabidopsis thaliana AGO1 and Drosophila melanogaster PIWI places seven AGOs in the AGO clade: ALG-1, ALG-2, ALG-3, ALG-4, ALG-5, ERGO-1, and RDE-1
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis performed by the authors

claim: A single C. elegans AGO belongs to the PIWI clade: PRG-1
source: a single AGO in the PIWI clade: PRG-1
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis performed by the authors

claim: 13 C. elegans AGOs belong to the WAGO clade
source: and 13 AGOs in the WAGO clade: CSR-1, C04F12.1 (renamed VSRA-1 for Versatile Small RNAs Argonaute-1, see below), WAGO-1, PPW-2/WAGO-3, WAGO-4, SAGO-2/WAGO-6, PPW-1/WAGO-7, SAGO-1/WAGO-8, HRDE-1/WAGO-9, WAGO-10, and NRDE-3/WAGO-12
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis performed by the authors

claim: CSR-1 exists as two isoforms: a long isoform (CSR-1a) and a short isoform (CSR-1b) that differ by 163 amino acids at their N terminus
source: It is important to note that CSR-1 exists as two isoforms, a long isoform (CSR-1a) and a short isoform (CSR-1b), that differ by 163 amino acids at their N terminus (Nguyen and Phillips, 2021; Charlesworth et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nguyen and Phillips, 2021 and Charlesworth et al., 2021

claim: GFP::3xFLAG tagged WAGO-1 did not behave as wild-type in phenotypic assays
source: Of all the AGOs tested, the GFP::3xFLAG tagged AGOs WAGO-1 and NRDE-3 did not behave as wild-type in phenotypic assays (Figure 1C and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and H with functional validation assays

claim: GFP::3xFLAG tagged NRDE-3 did not behave as wild-type in phenotypic assays
source: Of all the AGOs tested, the GFP::3xFLAG tagged AGOs WAGO-1 and NRDE-3 did not behave as wild-type in phenotypic assays (Figure 1C and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and H with functional validation assays

claim: 3xFLAG tagged WAGO-1 was functional in phenotypic assays
source: Both 3xFLAG tagged AGOs were functional in phenotypic assays (Figure 1C and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with functional validation assays

claim: 3xFLAG tagged NRDE-3 was functional in phenotypic assays
source: Both 3xFLAG tagged AGOs were functional in phenotypic assays (Figure 1C and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H with functional validation assays

claim: PPW-2 and WAGO-1 are N-terminally processed by the protease DPF-1
source: We note that although PPW-2 (also known as WAGO-3) and WAGO-1 were recently shown to be N-terminally processed by the protease DPF-1, both GFP::3xFLAG::PPW-2 and 3xFLAG::WAGO-1 strains behaved as wild-type, consistent with previous reports (Gudipati et al., 2021; Schreier et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gudipati et al., 2021 and Schreier et al., 2022

claim: ALG-1 associates primarily with miRNAs (~98% of reads)
source: For ALG-1, miRNAs comprised ~98% of all associated reads (47 miRNAs enriched)
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from ALG-1 IPs

claim: ALG-2 associates primarily with miRNAs (~98% of reads)
source: ALG-2, ~98% (81 enriched)
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from ALG-2 IPs

claim: ALG-5 associates primarily with miRNAs (~68% of reads)
source: ALG-5, ~68% (37 enriched)
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from ALG-5 IPs

claim: RDE-1 associates with miRNAs (~53% of reads)
source: and RDE-1, ~53% (103 enriched).
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from RDE-1 IPs

claim: RDE-1 associates with 22G-RNAs targeting protein-coding genes (~21% of reads, 536 enriched genes)
source: RDE-1 is involved in exoRNAi (Tabara et al., 1999); however, we observed that it also associates with 22G-RNAs targeting protein-coding genes (~21%, 536 enriched genes).
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from RDE-1 IPs

claim: ALG-3 associates with miRNAs (~55% of reads, 26 enriched)
source: We also detected abundant miRNAs associated with the rest of the AGO clade AGOs ALG-3, ALG-4, and ERGO-1, with ~55% (26 enriched)
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from ALG-3 IPs

claim: ALG-4 associates with miRNAs (~40% of reads, 2 enriched)
source: ~40% (2 enriched)
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from ALG-4 IPs

claim: ERGO-1 associates with miRNAs (~26% of reads, 33 enriched)
source: and ~26% (33 enriched) of reads corresponding to miRNAs, respectively.
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from ERGO-1 IPs

claim: ALG-3 associates with 26G-RNAs (~17% of reads)
source: Indeed, ALG-3, ALG-4, and ERGO-1 all associate with 26G-RNAs with ~17, 32, and 15% of reads corresponding to 26G-RNAs respectively
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from ALG-3 IPs

claim: ALG-4 associates with 26G-RNAs (~32% of reads)
source: Indeed, ALG-3, ALG-4, and ERGO-1 all associate with 26G-RNAs with ~17, 32, and 15% of reads corresponding to 26G-RNAs respectively
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from ALG-4 IPs

claim: ERGO-1 associates with 26G-RNAs (~15% of reads)
source: Indeed, ALG-3, ALG-4, and ERGO-1 all associate with 26G-RNAs with ~17, 32, and 15% of reads corresponding to 26G-RNAs respectively
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from ERGO-1 IPs

claim: PRG-1 is the major piRNA-associated AGO with ~64% of reads corresponding to piRNAs (5932 enriched)
source: It is the major piRNA-associated AGO, and ~64% of the reads in PRG-1 IPs correspond to piRNAs (5932 enriched)
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from PRG-1 IPs

claim: PRG-1 associates with 22G-RNAs (~21%) that primarily target protein-coding genes (150 gene targets enriched)
source: We also detected 22G-RNAs (~21%) that primarily targeted protein-coding genes enriched in PRG-1 complexes (150 gene targets enriched).
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from PRG-1 IPs

claim: 22G-RNAs are the most abundant class of small RNAs associated with the WAGOs
source: Previous studies predicted that all WAGOs would associate with 22G-RNAs (Guang et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2009; Buckley et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2018), and we observed that 22G-RNAs are the most abundant class of small RNAs associated with the WAGOs
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from WAGO IPs

claim: 190 miRNAs were found to be enriched over twofold in AGO IPs
source: We detected reads for 402 miRNAs across our AGO Input and IP samples. Of these, 190 were found to be enriched over twofold in the AGO IPs.
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from AGO IPs

claim: 103 miRNAs were enriched in RDE-1 complexes, with 55 being exclusive to RDE-1
source: For example, 103 miRNAs were enriched in RDE-1 complexes, with 55 being exclusive to RDE-1.
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from RDE-1 IPs

claim: The majority (63/103) of miRNAs enriched in RDE-1 were not conserved with C. briggsae
source: RDE-1 was the only AGO where the majority (63/103) of enriched miRNAs were not conserved with those of the related nematode, Caenorhabditis briggsae
evidence: This is based on analysis of miRNA conservation

claim: Newly evolved miRNAs may be routed initially into the RDE-1 pathway before subsequently integrating into the ALG-1/2/5 pathway
source: suggesting that newly evolved miRNAs may be routed initially into the RDE-1 pathway before subsequently integrating into the ALG-1/2/5 pathway
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RDE-1 enriches for non-conserved miRNAs

claim: miRNAs loaded into RDE-1 showed a lower average of mismatches in their precursors compared to those loaded into ALG-1, ALG-2, and ALG-5
source: miRNAs loaded into RDE-1 showed a lower average of mismatches in their precursors, and miRNAs derived from precursors with no mismatches were only bound by RDE-1
evidence: This is based on analysis of precursor miRNA sequences shown in Figure 3B

claim: Endogenous miRNAs with higher complementarity in their precursor duplex are preferentially loaded into RDE-1
source: These data suggest that endogenous miRNAs with higher complementarity in their precursor duplex are preferentially loaded into RDE-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of precursor miRNA mismatches

claim: AGO-enriched miRNAs were substantially depleted in alg-1, alg-2, alg-5, and rde-1 mutants
source: We found that the AGO-enriched miRNAs were substantially depleted in alg-1, alg-2, alg-5, and rde-1 mutants (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from ago mutants shown in Figure 3C

claim: Loss of ALG-1 had the most substantial effect on global miRNA levels, leading to a greater than twofold decrease
source: Loss of ALG-1 had the most substantial effect on global miRNA levels, leading to a greater than twofold decrease (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from alg-1 mutants shown in Figure 3D

claim: alg-1 is genetically required for the stability of most miRNAs
source: indicating that alg-1 is genetically required for the stability of most miRNAs and potentially explaining why alg-1 mutants have more severe phenotypes than the other miRNA-associated ago mutants (Bukhari et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of ALG-1 causes the largest decrease in global miRNA levels

claim: ERGO-1 physically interacts with both ALG-1 and ALG-2
source: We found that ERGO-1 physically interacted with both ALG-1 and ALG-2 (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is based on co-IP experiments shown in Figure 3E

claim: ERGO-1 interacts with ALG-1 and ALG-2 in an RNA-dependent manner
source: in an RNA-dependent manner (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on co-IP experiments with RNase treatment shown in Figure 3F

claim: miRNAs were substantially reduced in ERGO-1 IPs after RNase treatment, while 26G-RNAs remained enriched
source: we sequenced sRNAs associated with ERGO-1 IPs after RNase treatment and observed that miRNAs were substantially reduced, while 26G-RNAs remained enriched, compared to non-RNase treated ERGO-1 IPs (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from RNase-treated ERGO-1 IPs shown in Figure 3G and H

claim: alg-1; ergo-1 double mutants appeared sickly, being smaller and more pale than wild-type animals, with many dying prematurely
source: alg-1; ergo-1 double mutants appeared sickly, being smaller and more pale than wild-type animals, with many dying prematurely, and only ~4% of the animals surviving past the L4 stage, compared to ~45% and 100% for alg-1 and ergo-1 single mutants, respectively (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is based on phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 3I

claim: alg-1 and ergo-1 genetically interact to ensure survival into adulthood
source: These data indicate that alg-1 and ergo-1 genetically interact to ensure survival into adulthood
evidence: This is inferred from the severe phenotype of alg-1; ergo-1 double mutants

claim: 10 putative, high-confidence miRNAs were found in ALG-1 and ALG-2 complexes using mirDeep2 analysis
source: We used the miRNA prediction program mirDeep2 to analyze sequencing data from the miRNA binding AGO IPs (Friedländer et al., 2008). We found 10 putative, high-confidence miRNAs (Supplementary file 5) present in ALG-1 and ALG-2 complexes.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of small RNA sequencing data

claim: 5 of the 10 putative miRNAs were significantly depleted in alg-1 or alg-2 mutants
source: Consistent with these being bona fide miRNAs, 5 of the 10 putative miRNAs were significantly depleted in alg-1 or alg-2 mutants (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from ago mutants shown in Figure 3K

claim: Five sRNAs annotated as miRNAs (cel-miR-4936, cel-miR-8198-3p, cel-miR-8202-5p, cel-miR-78, and cel-miR-798) are mis-annotated piRNAs
source: We found three likely mis-annotated miRNAs (cel-miR-4936, cel-miR-8198-3p, and cel-miR-8202-5p) enriched in IPs of the Piwi AGO, PRG-1, consistent with a previous report of two similarly mis-annotated miRNAs (cel-miR-78 and cel-miR-798) (Batista et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on enrichment in PRG-1 IPs and depletion in prg-1 mutants

claim: All five mis-annotated miRNAs were depleted over 60-fold on average in prg-1 mutants
source: All five miRNAs were depleted over 60-fold on average in prg-1 mutants
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from prg-1 mutants

claim: prg-1 is required to maintain piRNA pools globally, with an ~13.9-fold reduction in piRNA levels overall
source: The levels of piRNAs in ago mutants revealed that prg-1 is required to maintain piRNA pools globally, with an ~13.9-fold reduction in piRNA levels overall (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is based on small RNA sequencing data from prg-1 mutants shown in Figure 4B

claim: 466 previously uncharacterized piRNAs were identified
source: In total, we found 466 sequences that were 21U, enriched over twofold in both PRG-1 IP replicates, and were not perfectly matching to annotated piRNA sequences. All of these 21U sRNAs were depleted, and 222 were significantly depleted, in prg-1 mutants compared to wild-type (Figure 4E, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on analysis of 21U sRNAs enriched in PRG-1 IPs and depleted in prg-1 mutants

claim: Most of the 466 novel piRNA sequences (375/466) originated from a piRNA cluster spanning coordinates 4.5–7.0M on chromosome IV
source: and most of these sequences (375/466) originated from a previously described piRNA cluster that spanned coordinates 4.5–7.0M on chromosome IV (Ruby et al., 2006; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of genomic locations of novel piRNAs shown in Figure 4G

claim: 10,127 protein-coding genes had sRNAs that were enriched at least twofold in association with at least one AGO
source: A total of 10,127 genes had sRNAs that were enriched at least twofold in association with at least one AGO, indicating that at least half of the protein-coding genome has the potential to be regulated by AGO/sRNA complexes at this developmental stage.
evidence: This is based on analysis of small RNA sequencing data from AGO IPs

claim: Hierarchical clustering of enriched target genes enabled identification of four clear clusters of AGOs
source: Hierarchical clustering of the enriched target genes of each AGO enabled us to identify four clear clusters of AGOs that target similar sets of protein-coding genes and could therefore function together in regulating those genes (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: The WAGO cluster consists of WAGO-1, PPW-2, HRDE-1, and PPW-1
source: The first AGO cluster consists of the WAGOs WAGO-1 (1814 targets), PPW-2 (636 targets), HRDE-1 (1295 targets), and PPW-1 (870 targets) (Figure 5A), which we term the WAGO cluster.
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: The ERGO-1 cluster consists of ERGO-1, PPW-1, SAGO-1, SAGO-2, and NRDE-3
source: The second AGO cluster consists of the AGOs SAGO-2 (1537 targets), SAGO-1 (181 targets), ERGO-1 (239 targets), and NRDE-3 (116 targets) (Figure 5A), which we term the ERGO-1 cluster.
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: The CSR-1 cluster consists of CSR-1, WAGO-4, and C04F12.1/VSRA-1
source: The third cluster consists of the WAGOs CSR-1 (4182 targets), WAGO-4 (4815 targets), and C04F12.1/VSRA-1 (1797 targets) (Figure 5A), which we term the CSR-1 cluster.
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: The ALG-3/4 cluster consists of RDE-1, WAGO-10, ALG-3, and ALG-4
source: The fourth cluster consists of the AGOs RDE-1 (388 targets), WAGO-10 (877 targets), ALG-3 (2966 targets), and ALG-4 (3378 targets) (Figure 5A), which we term the ALG-3/4 cluster.
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: 490 pseudogenes were enriched with antisense sRNAs across AGO IP data sets
source: We detected sRNA reads against 1741 out of 2124 annotated pseudogenes and found that 490 were enriched with antisense sRNAs across our IP data sets.
evidence: This is based on analysis of small RNA sequencing data from AGO IPs

claim: 150 transposable elements were enriched for antisense sRNAs across AGO IP data sets
source: We detected reads against all 163 annotated transposable elements. Of these, 150 were enriched for antisense sRNAs across our IP data sets (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of small RNA sequencing data from AGO IPs shown in Figure 5E

claim: All transposable elements have the potential to be regulated by sRNAs
source: This indicates that all transposable elements have the potential to be regulated by sRNAs and that most of them are likely to be highly regulated by AGO/sRNA complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that reads were detected against all 163 annotated transposable elements

claim: The WAGO cluster is the major regulator of transposable elements, particularly in the germline
source: Most transposable elements (134) are targeted by the WAGO cluster AGOs, with 104 of these being unique to this cluster (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B). This suggests that the WAGO cluster is the major regulator of transposable elements, particularly in the germline.
evidence: This is based on analysis of transposable element targeting shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: 60 lincRNAs were enriched for antisense sRNAs across AGO IP data sets
source: We detected reads against 168 of the 191 annotated lincRNAs (defined in Nam and Bartel, 2012 and WormBase version WS276), across all IP data sets, and, among these, 60 of these were enriched for antisense sRNAs (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of small RNA sequencing data from AGO IPs shown in Figure 5F

claim: Loss of PRG-1 led to downregulation of secondary sRNAs associated with the WAGO cluster AGOs
source: Loss of the piRNA-binding primary AGO PRG-1, which results in the loss of most piRNAs (Figure 4B), led to downregulation of secondary sRNAs associated with the WAGO cluster AGOs sRNAs (Montgomery et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on analysis of small RNA sequencing data from prg-1 mutants

claim: Loss of ERGO-1 resulted in the loss of ERGO-1 cluster sRNAs
source: loss of the 26G-RNA-binding primary AGO ERGO-1 resulted in the loss of ERGO-1 cluster sRNAs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of small RNA sequencing data from ergo-1 mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: SAGO-1- and SAGO-2-associated 22G-RNAs are depleted upon loss of ERGO-1
source: Our complete analysis reveals that SAGO-1- and SAGO-2-associated 22G-RNAs are depleted upon loss of ERGO-1, indicating that SAGO-1 and SAGO-2 also work within the context of ERGO-1 targeting.
evidence: This is based on analysis of small RNA sequencing data from ergo-1 mutants

claim: PPW-1 acts downstream of both the PRG-1 piRNA pathway and the ERGO-1 26G-RNA pathway
source: When taken together with the clustering analysis of targets (Figure 5A and D–F), it appears that PPW-1 acts downstream of both the PRG-1 piRNA pathway and the ERGO-1 26G-RNA pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PPW-1-bound sRNAs are depleted in both prg-1 and ergo-1 mutants depending on the target type

claim: C04F12.1/VSRA-1 acts downstream of ERGO-1 26G-RNAs to target pseudogenes, transposons, and lincRNAs, and acts in conjunction with CSR-1 22G-RNAs to target protein-coding genes in the germline
source: C04F12.1/VSRA-1 acts downstream of ERGO-1 26G-RNAs to target pseudogenes, transposons, and lincRNAs, and acts in conjunction with CSR-1 22G-RNAs to target protein-coding genes in the germline (Figure 5A and D–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from clustering analysis and mutant sRNA sequencing data

claim: Loss of both CSR-1 isoforms in a null mutant resulted in depletion of CSR-1 cluster sRNAs targeting protein-coding genes
source: Loss of both isoforms of CSR-1 in a null mutant resulted in depletion of CSR-1 cluster sRNAs targeting protein-coding genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is based on analysis of small RNA sequencing data from csr-1 mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: Loss of HRDE-1 resulted in depletion of WAGO-1- and HRDE-1-associated sRNAs
source: loss of HRDE-1 alone also resulted in depletion of WAGO-1- and HRDE-1-associated sRNAs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of small RNA sequencing data from hrde-1 mutants

claim: HRDE-1 is required for the stability of most of the WAGO cluster associated sRNAs
source: This indicates that HRDE-1 is required for the stability of most of the WAGO cluster associated sRNAs, likely reflecting the requirement of HRDE-1 in producing tertiary sRNAs (Sapetschnig et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of HRDE-1 depletes WAGO cluster sRNAs

claim: 16 out of 19 AGOs are expressed in the germline
source: We identified 16/19 AGOs expressed in the germline, consistent with known roles for AGOs in the germline (Figure 6A and F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations shown in Figure 6A and F

claim: Eight AGOs show germline-restricted expression
source: Eight of these show germline-restricted expression and the other eight are also expressed in somatic tissues (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–8).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations shown in Figure 7F and supplementary figures

claim: 11 out of 19 AGOs are expressed in the soma
source: In total, 11/19 AGOs are expressed in the soma, with 3 AGOs being somatically restricted (SAGO-1, SAGO-2, ALG-1) (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–8).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations shown in Figure 7F and supplementary figures

claim: Nine AGOs are constitutively expressed throughout the germline from the emergence of the P1 cell through spermatogenesis to oogenesis: RDE-1, ALG-5, PRG-1, CSR-1b, WAGO-1, PPW-2, WAGO-4, PPW-1, and HRDE-1
source: Nine AGOs are constitutively expressed throughout the germline from the emergence of the P1 cell through spermatogenesis in the L4 stage to oogenesis in adults: RDE-1, ALG-5, PRG-1, CSR-1b, WAGO-1, PPW-2, WAGO-4, PPW-1, and HRDE-1 (Figure 6F, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–8).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations throughout development

claim: ALG-3, ALG-4, WAGO-10, and CSR-1a are expressed only during spermatogenesis
source: ALG-3, ALG-4, WAGO-10, and the CSR-1a isoform are expressed only during spermatogenesis, at the L4 stage in hermaphrodites and constitutively in the male germline (Charlesworth et al., 2021; Nguyen and Phillips, 2021; Figure 6A, Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations shown in Figure 6A, Figure 7F, and Figure 7—figure supplement 7

claim: ALG-2, ERGO-1, and NRDE-3 are specifically expressed in oocytes starting at the young adult hermaphrodite stage
source: ALG-2, ERGO-1, and NRDE-3 are specifically expressed in oocytes starting at the young adult hermaphrodite stage (Figure 6A and F).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations shown in Figure 6A and F

claim: Eight germline AGOs are enriched in perinuclear phase-separated germ granules: ALG-3, ALG-4, ALG-5, PRG-1, CSR-1a, CSR-1b, WAGO-1, PPW-2, and WAGO-4
source: Half (8/16) of the germline AGOs are enriched in perinuclear phase-separated germ granules: ALG-3, ALG-4, ALG-5, PRG-1, CSR-1a, b, WAGO-1, PPW-2, and WAGO-4 (Figure 6A and F).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations shown in Figure 6A and F

claim: CSR-1 and WAGO-4 overlapped roughly equally with both P and Z granule pixels
source: The CSR-1 cluster AGOs CSR-1 and WAGO-4 overlapped roughly equally with both P and Z granule pixels, whereas the WAGO cluster AGOs PPW-2 and WAGO-1 were strongly biased toward overlap with P granules (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on quantification of pixel overlap shown in Figure 6B

claim: PPW-2 and WAGO-1 were strongly biased toward overlap with P granules
source: whereas the WAGO cluster AGOs PPW-2 and WAGO-1 were strongly biased toward overlap with P granules (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on quantification of pixel overlap shown in Figure 6B

claim: HRDE-1 and NRDE-3 are predominantly nuclear AGOs
source: Two AGOs are predominantly nuclear: HRDE-1 and NRDE-3 (Figure 6A and F).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations shown in Figure 6A and F

claim: At 20°C, seven ago mutants showed compromised fertility: alg-1, alg-2, alg-5, ergo-1, prg-1, rde-1, and wago-1
source: At 20°C, seven ago mutants showed compromised fertility: alg-1, alg-2, alg-5, ergo-1, prg-1, rde-1, and wago-1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on brood size assays shown in Figure 6D

claim: At 25°C, fertility defects were observed for alg-4, ppw-2, wago-4, and hrde-1 mutants that were not present at 20°C
source: We also observed fertility defects not present at 20°C for four ago mutants: alg-4, ppw-2, wago-4, and hrde-1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on brood size assays shown in Figure 6D

claim: More than half (10/19) of the C. elegans AGOs contribute individually to optimal fertility
source: These results indicate that more than half (10/19) of the C. elegans AGOs contribute individually to optimal fertility.
evidence: This is inferred from the brood size assays showing fertility defects in 10 ago mutants

claim: Complete loss of fertility over varied numbers of generations at 25°C was observed for alg-5 (25 generations), rde-1 (24), prg-1 (8), wago-1 (11), ppw-2 (5), wago-4 (5), and hrde-1 (4)
source: We observed complete loss of fertility over varied numbers of generations for alg-5 (25 generations), rde-1 (24), prg-1 (8), wago-1 (11), ppw-2 (5), wago-4 (5), and hrde-1 (4) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on Mortal germline assays shown in Figure 6E

claim: The Mrt phenotype of wago-1, ppw-2, wago-4, and hrde-1 mutants is reversible upon transferring animals back to 20°C
source: We maintained animals at 25°C for three generations, then transferred them back to 20°C and measured brood size at each generation. For all four mutants, we observed the same pattern; a reversal of the Mrt phenotype (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is based on temperature shift experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A

claim: Mrt wago mutants produced fewer germ cells than wild-type controls at the mitotic zone
source: Counting germ cells at the mitotic zone at 20°C and 25°C revealed Mrt wagos produced fewer germ cells than wild-type controls, suggesting a proliferation defect (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on counting germ cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B

claim: The intestine expresses the most AGOs in somatic tissue: ALG-1, ALG-2, ERGO-1, RDE-1, CSR-1a, PPW-1, SAGO-2, SAGO-1, and NRDE-3
source: The intestine is the somatic tissue that expresses the most AGOs: ALG-1, ALG-2, ERGO-1, RDE-1, CSR-1a (the long isoform of CSR-1), PPW-1, SAGO-2, SAGO-1, and NRDE-3 (Figure 7A and B, Figure 7—figure supplement 8; Guang et al., 2008; Vasquez-Rifo et al., 2013; Charlesworth et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations shown in Figure 7A and B

claim: SAGO-1, SAGO-2, and PPW-1 show accumulation along the apical membrane of intestinal cells
source: Most AGOs were broadly cytoplasmic; NRDE-3 was nuclear; and three AGOs, SAGO-1, SAGO-2, and PPW-1, showed an accumulation along the apical membrane of the intestinal cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy observations shown in Figure 7B

claim: sago-2 and ppw-1 mutants are partially resistant to killing by PA14 infection
source: In agreement, survival assays of sago-2, ppw-1, and sago-1 mutants on PA14 revealed that both sago-2 and ppw-1 are partially resistant to killing by PA14 infection (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on PA14 survival assays shown in Figure 7D

claim: sago-2 mutants showed a higher Orsay virus infection level that phenocopied rde-1 mutants
source: Only sago-2 showed a higher infection level, which phenocopied that of rde-1 mutants (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on Orsay virus infection assays shown in Figure 7E

claim: SAGO-2 may have dual roles in mediating immunity in the intestine
source: Thus, SAGO-2 may have dual roles in mediating immunity in the intestine. First, SAGO-2 targets immune response genes, and loss of sago-2 enhances the ability of the worms to survive on PA14. Conversely, loss of sago-2 decreases viral RNA targeting, likely by RNAi mechanisms in which SAGO-2 is loaded with secondary 22G-RNAs that were generated after targeting of viral RNA by the primary AGO RDE-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that sago-2 mutants are resistant to PA14 but sensitive to Orsay virus
